episodes.title: Why does music give you chills?
episodes.hook: Why does your favorite song give you goosebumps?
episodes.twist: Your brain starts releasing dopamine in anticipation, seconds before the best part even arrives.
sources: Salimpoor, Benovoy, Larcher, Dagher & Zatorre (2011), 'Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music', Nature Neuroscience 14, 257-262, doi:10.1038/nn.2726, https://www.nature.com/articles/nn.2726 (dopamine is released at peak musical pleasure; the caudate is active in the anticipation before the peak, the nucleus accumbens during it; chills were the marker of peak emotion)

Shwartz et al. (2020), 'Cell types promoting goosebumps form a niche to regulate hair follicle stem cells', Cell 182(3), 578-593, Harvard / Hsu lab, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32679029/ (goosebumps happen when sympathetic nerves make the tiny arrector pili muscle at each hair follicle contract, pulling the hair upright)

episodes.title: Why are yawns contagious?
episodes.hook: Why do you yawn just from seeing someone else yawn?
episodes.twist: How easily you catch a yawn depends on how excitable your brain's movement area is, and trying to hold it in makes the urge stronger.
sources: Brown et al. (2017), 'A neural basis for contagious yawning', Current Biology 27(17), 2713-2717, University of Nottingham, https://eprints.nottingham.ac.uk/44492 (motor-cortex excitability predicts how readily people yawn after seeing others yawn; brain stimulation raised the urge)

University of Nottingham press release (Aug 2017), 'Yawning: why is it so contagious and why should it matter?', https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/news/pressreleases/2017/august/yawning-why-is-it-so-contagious-and-why-should-it-matter.aspx (contagious yawning is an automatic copying reflex triggered by seeing someone yawn; being told to resist increased the urge)

episodes.title: Why does ice cream freeze your brain?
episodes.hook: Why does ice cream make your whole head hurt?
episodes.twist: The pain isn't the cold itself: a brain artery suddenly widens to rush warm blood in, then narrows again as the pain fades.
sources: Serrador et al. (2012), Experimental Biology 2012 abstract, Harvard Medical School / VA; American Physiological Society release, https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/816505 (sipping ice water against the palate made the anterior cerebral artery dilate rapidly as the pain began and constrict as it eased; 13 volunteers)

ScienceDaily (Apr 2012), 'Brain freeze: new insight into headaches', https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/04/120422231742.htm (same study: sudden increase in blood flow through the anterior cerebral artery tracked the brain-freeze pain; suggested role keeping the brain warm)

episodes.title: Why can't you tickle yourself?
episodes.hook: Try tickling yourself right now. Nothing, right?
episodes.twist: Your brain predicts your own touch before it happens and turns the feeling down, but add a tiny delay and it starts to tickle again.
sources: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998), 'Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation', Nature Neuroscience 1(7), 635-640, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/2870 (self-produced touch is rated less tickly than identical external touch; the cerebellum's prediction cancels the response)

Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999), 'Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli', Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5), 551-559, https://wolpertlab.neuroscience.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/content/papers/BlaWolFri99.pdf (adding a delay between your movement and the touch makes self-touch feel more ticklish)

episodes.title: Why do you get hiccups?
episodes.hook: Why does your body randomly go 'hic'?
episodes.twist: The 'hic' is your vocal cords snapping shut, and one theory says the whole reflex is a leftover from our ancestors' tadpole-like breathing.
sources: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine), 'Hiccups', https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003068.htm (a hiccup is an involuntary movement of the diaphragm followed by quick closing of the vocal cords, which makes the 'hic' sound)

Straus et al. (2003), 'A phylogenetic hypothesis for the origin of hiccough', BioEssays 25(2), 182-188, doi:10.1002/bies.10224, https://core.ac.uk/download/357378668.pdf (proposes hiccups are a leftover of the gill-ventilation pattern of amphibian tadpoles; a hypothesis, said as 'one theory')

episodes.title: Why do songs get stuck in your head?
episodes.hook: Why does one song play in your head all day?
episodes.twist: Earworms tend to be fast, simple tunes with one surprising jump, and chewing gum keeps your 'inner voice' busy so they show up less.
sources: Jakubowski, Finkel, Stewart & Müllensiefen (2016), 'Dissecting an earworm: Melodic features and song popularity predict involuntary musical imagery', Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, APA press release https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2016/11/earworms (earworms are usually faster, with a common, easy melodic shape plus unusual intervals such as leaps or repeats)

Beaman, Powell & Rapley (2015), 'Want to block earworms from conscious awareness? B(u)y gum!', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 68(6), 1049-1057, University of Reading, https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/40114/ (chewing gum reduced unwanted musical thoughts, more than finger tapping did)

episodes.title: Why do you feel better after crying?
episodes.hook: Why does a good cry make you feel lighter?
episodes.twist: Right after a cry your mood can dip, but about an hour and a half later people who cried felt better than before they started.
sources: Gračanin, Bylsma & Vingerhoets (2014), 'Is crying a self-soothing behavior?', Frontiers in Psychology 5:502, https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00502/full (review: converging evidence that crying has self-soothing effects, proposed via parasympathetic nervous system activation and oxytocin)

Gračanin, Vingerhoets, Kardum, Zupčić, Šantek & Šimić (2015), 'Why crying does and sometimes does not seem to alleviate mood: a quasi-experimental study', Motivation and Emotion 39(6), 953-960, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4608976 (criers' mood dipped right after a sad film, returned to baseline within 20 min, and was better than before at 90 min)

episodes.title: Why do you shake when you're nervous?
episodes.hook: Why do your hands shake right before you go on stage?
episodes.twist: Nerves and excitement feel almost the same in the body, and people who told themselves 'I'm excited' actually did better.
sources: Harvard Health Publishing, 'Understanding the stress response', https://www.health.harvard.edu/staying-healthy/understanding-the-stress-response (in fight-or-flight the adrenal glands pump adrenaline into the blood: the heart beats faster, breathing speeds up, muscles tense)

Brooks, A. W. (2014), 'Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement', Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 143(3), 1144-1158, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24364682/ (anxiety and excitement are both high-arousal states; saying 'I am excited' improved singing, speaking and math performance compared with trying to calm down)

episodes.title: Why is laughing so contagious?
episodes.hook: Why do you start laughing just because your friend is?
episodes.twist: Hearing a laugh makes your brain quietly get your face muscles ready to smile, before you even decide to.
sources: Warren et al. (2006), 'Positive emotions preferentially engage an auditory-motor mirror system', Journal of Neuroscience 26(50), 13067-13075, UCL / Imperial College (hearing laughter activates the premotor cortex that prepares facial movement, more strongly than negative sounds)

Nature news (12 Dec 2006), 'Laughter really is contagious', doi:10.1038/news061211-7, https://www.nature.com/news/2006/061211/full/news061211-7.html (same study: the premotor response to laughter and cheering was larger, an automatic mirroring that may help social bonding)

episodes.title: Why does being left out hurt so much?
episodes.hook: Why does being left out feel like it actually hurts?
episodes.twist: Your brain uses some of the same alarm areas for being left out as for physical pain, because belonging always mattered for survival.
sources: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003), 'Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion', Science 302(5643), 290-292, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14551436/ (being excluded from a ball-tossing game activated the anterior cingulate cortex, a region also involved in physical pain, and activity tracked distress)

Kross, Berman, Mischel, Smith & Wager (2011), 'Social rejection shares somatosensory representations with physical pain', PNAS 108(15), 6270-6275, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21444827/ (recalling a recent rejection activated regions that also responded to physical pain; the overlap is debated, so we say 'some of the same areas')

episodes.title: Why do hugs feel so good?
episodes.hook: Why does one good hug make everything feel lighter?
episodes.twist: Your skin has special nerves tuned to slow, gentle touch, and people who got more hugs got less sick when stressed.
sources: Löken, Wessberg, Morrison, McGlone & Olausson (2009), 'Coding of pleasant touch by unmyelinated afferents in humans', Nature Neuroscience 12, 547-548, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19363489/ (C-tactile nerve fibres respond best to slow, gentle stroking, and their firing tracks how pleasant the touch feels)

Cohen, Janicki-Deverts, Turner & Doyle (2015), 'Does hugging provide stress-buffering social support?', Psychological Science 26(2), 135-147, Carnegie Mellon, https://www.cmu.edu/news/stories/archives/2014/december/december17_hugsprotect.html (more frequent hugs were linked to less severe cold symptoms in people exposed to a cold virus, and accounted for a third of social support's protective effect)

episodes.title: What a crush does to your brain
episodes.hook: When you like someone, your brain lights up like you won a prize.
episodes.twist: Scientists found a crush works less like an emotion and more like a motivation, the same reward system that makes you want things.
sources: Aron, Fisher, Mashek, Strong, Li & Brown (2005), 'Reward, motivation, and emotion systems associated with early-stage intense romantic love', Journal of Neurophysiology 94(1), 327-337, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15928068/ (looking at the beloved activated the dopamine-rich ventral tegmental area and caudate; the authors describe early love as a motivation system)

Fisher, Aron & Brown (2005), 'Romantic love: An fMRI study of a neural mechanism for mate choice', Journal of Comparative Neurology 493(1), 58-62, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16255001/ (early-stage romantic love activates reward and motivation pathways, especially the VTA and caudate)

episodes.title: Why can't you stop thinking about your crush?
episodes.hook: Why does your crush live in your head rent-free?
episodes.twist: In early love, one study found a serotonin marker in the blood at levels like those in people with obsessive thoughts, so a crush on repeat is your brain chemistry, not you being weird.
sources: Marazziti, Akiskal, Rossi & Cassano (1999), 'Alteration of the platelet serotonin transporter in romantic love', Psychological Medicine 29(3), 741-745, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10405096/ (20 people who had fallen in love within 6 months had platelet serotonin transporter density similar to OCD patients and lower than controls)

Fisher, Aron & Brown (2006), 'Romantic love: a mammalian brain system for mate choice', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 361(1476), 2173-2186, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1764845/ (the most characteristic trait of romantic love: the lover thinks obsessively about the beloved, 'intrusive thinking')

episodes.title: Your eyes give your crush away
episodes.hook: Your eyes do something you can't control when you see someone you like.
episodes.twist: Your pupils widen when you look at something that interests or excites you, and you can't stop them, because the nervous system does it on its own.
sources: Hess & Polt (1960), 'Pupil size as related to interest value of visual stimuli', Science 132(3423), 349-350, doi:10.1126/science.132.3423.349 (pupils enlarge when people view emotionally toned or interesting pictures)

de Winter, Petermeijer, Kooijman & Dodou (2021), 'Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess', International Journal of Psychophysiology, TU Delft, https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/a4c89e29-c26e-4e94-b2ac-53d86e6f1969 (modern replication confirmed pupils dilate to arousing stimuli; Hess's mimicry and gender claims did not replicate, so we only say 'interest')

episodes.title: What holding hands does to two brains
episodes.hook: When two people hold hands, their brains do something wild.
episodes.twist: Their brain waves start to sync up, and in one study the more in sync they were, the less pain the other person felt.
sources: Goldstein, Weissman-Fogel, Dumas & Shamay-Tsoory (2018), 'Brain-to-brain coupling during handholding is associated with pain reduction', PNAS (Feb 2018), https://www.pasteur.fr/en/node/7654 (Institut Pasteur summary: 22 couples; brain-wave coupling rose most when they held hands during pain, and greater coupling went with less pain)

ScienceDaily / University of Colorado Boulder (1 Mar 2018), 'Holding hands can sync brainwaves, ease pain, study shows', https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/03/180301094822.htm (same study: hand-holding increased brain-wave coupling; the more empathic the partner, the more in sync and the less pain)

episodes.title: Why do you forget words around your crush?
episodes.hook: Why does your brain go blank the second your crush says hi?
episodes.twist: A rush of stress chemicals briefly turns down your brain's planning area, so going blank means you care, not that you're awkward.
sources: Arnsten, A. F. T. (2009), 'Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function', Nature Reviews Neuroscience 10(6), 410-422, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2907136/ (even mild acute stress rapidly impairs prefrontal cognitive abilities via high norepinephrine and dopamine release)

Arnsten, A. F. T. (2015), 'Stress weakens prefrontal networks: molecular insults to higher cognition', Nature Neuroscience 18(10), 1376-1385, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4816215/ (acute stress quickly takes the prefrontal cortex 'offline', shifting control to more reflexive brain circuits; the effect is reversible)

episodes.title: Why can't you move in your dreams?
episodes.hook: Every night, your body switches off your muscles. On purpose.
episodes.twist: During dream sleep your brain blocks the signals to your muscles, so you can run in a dream without running into your wall.
sources: Brooks & Peever (2012), 'Identification of the transmitter and receptor mechanisms responsible for REM sleep paralysis', Journal of Neuroscience 32(29), 9785-9795, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6621291 (REM sleep paralysis is produced by GABA and glycine inhibition of motor neurons)

Society for Neuroscience (18 Jul 2012), 'Study identifies how muscles are paralyzed during sleep', https://www.sfn.org/publications/latest-news/2012/07/18/study-identifies-how-muscles-are-paralyzed-during-sleep (during REM sleep, when most dreaming happens, the muscles are paralysed, which keeps us from acting out our dreams)

episodes.title: Why can't teens fall asleep early?
episodes.hook: Why are you wide awake at midnight but a zombie at seven?
episodes.twist: It isn't laziness: in the teen years your body clock shifts later and your sleep hormone melatonin arrives later at night.
sources: Carskadon, M. A. (2011), 'Sleep in adolescents: the perfect storm', Pediatric Clinics of North America 58(3), 637-647, doi:10.1016/j.pcl.2011.03.003 (the circadian system shifts later during adolescence, including later melatonin secretion; teen sleep loss is not lower need)

Crowley, Wolfson, Tarokh & Carskadon (2018), 'An update on adolescent sleep: New evidence informing the perfect storm model', Journal of Adolescence 67, 55-65, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29908393/ (review confirming the later circadian phase and melatonin timing in adolescents)

episodes.title: Your brain cleans itself while you sleep
episodes.hook: While you sleep, your brain does the dishes.
episodes.twist: In sleeping mice, the spaces between brain cells opened up by about sixty percent so fluid could wash waste away much faster.
sources: Xie et al. (2013), 'Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain', Science 342(6156), 373-377, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/ (in mice, sleep increased the space between brain cells by about 60%, speeding the clearance of waste such as beta-amyloid)

National Institutes of Health news release (17 Oct 2013), 'Brain may flush out toxins during sleep', https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/brain-may-flush-out-toxins-during-sleep (NIH-funded study: sleep clears the brain of damaging molecules; findings in mice)

episodes.title: Why sleep helps you remember
episodes.hook: You studied all night, but your brain does the real saving after you fall asleep.
episodes.twist: While you sleep, your brain replays what you learned and moves it into longer-term storage, so sleep is part of studying.
sources: Diekelmann & Born (2010), 'The memory function of sleep', Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11(2), 114-126, doi:10.1038/nrn2762 (sleep optimises the consolidation of newly learned information, through reactivation of the activity patterns from learning)

Stickgold & Walker (2007), 'Sleep-dependent memory consolidation and reconsolidation', Sleep Medicine 8(4), 331-343, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2680680 (many steps of memory consolidation occur preferentially during sleep, stabilising new memories)
